Product Ecosystem Cases

When More Data Isn't the Answer

Product Analytics Decision Hub · Internal Product

Product teams had data, but no reliable system for turning it into decisions. Every new question required rebuilding definitions, context, and trust from scratch.

The problem

  • 01Different definitions: the same signal could mean something different depending on the team, dashboard, or person you asked.
  • 02Fragmented instrumentation: signals were tracked and named inconsistently, making it difficult to connect behavior across the product.
  • 03Missed the moment: teams often understood what a signal meant only after the decision it was supposed to inform had already been made.

The product tension

The real challenge wasn't producing more data. It was changing how teams used it.

Autonomy

Teams should be able to answer product questions independently.

↔

Trust & consistency

The same evidence should mean the same thing across teams.

The challenge was enabling teams to move faster, trust the same evidence, and find out in time to act on it.

How might we help product teams move from question to evidence independently, without sacrificing trust in the data?

Who I was building for

Product builders, CSMs, and Directors: the people shaping the roadmap, the people closest to what customers actually needed, and the people who had to defend prioritization calls without solid evidence underneath them.

The product loop

How I actually worked through this, end to end:

  1. 01
    Understand: Why wasn't data becoming part of product decisions?

    What I did: I started with a visibility hypothesis and looked at how other companies approached product analytics. The turning point came from digging into our own databases, dashboards, definitions, and data availability process.

    What I learned: The issue wasn't a lack of data. It was fragmented access, inconsistent definitions, and generic reporting that couldn't answer specific product questions.

    Key insight: This wasn't a dashboard problem. It was a fragmented system of access, meaning, and interpretation.
  2. 02
    Frame: Where should I intervene first?

    What I considered: Dynamic dashboards, a structured data layer, and improving how product data was defined and made available.

    What I decided: Start with the semantic layer and the data availability process. Building better dashboards on top of inconsistent definitions would only make the problem easier to see, not solve it.

    Key decision: Fix the meaning and reliability of the data before scaling how teams consume it.
  3. 03
    Build: What was the smallest system that could test the hypothesis?

    I built three connected pieces:

    01
    Shared meaning

    A semantic layer, made available through the Data Lake, so teams could work from the same product definitions and relationships.

    02
    Faster access

    A self-service instrumentation and data availability process designed to remove the long dependency chain between defining a signal and being able to use it.

    03
    Awareness & guidance

    A Product Analytics Hub, paired with a co-working agent, to help teams discover what existed, understand how to use it, and apply it to their own product questions.

    Key decision: Solve meaning, access, and interpretation as one connected system, not as three isolated tools.
  4. 04
    Test: How did we put it into real product work?

    What I tested: I worked with a pilot squad and key users, and redesigned one of the most-used dashboards using the new semantic logic.

    What changed: The goal shifted from simply showing the "right" data to surfacing the most relevant insights, adding guidance on how to interpret them, and connecting those insights to possible product decisions.

    Key learning: Reliable data is not enough. Teams need context to know what matters, how to read it, and what to do next.
  5. 05
    Learn: What did the evidence teach us, and what changed next?

    What I learned: The answer wasn't to build the perfect dashboard. Teams needed the semantic context, interpretation guidance, and access to evidence to make decisions themselves.

    What changed: I shifted the approach from creating centralized analytics outputs to enabling teams with a reusable decision system.

    Key learning: The product wasn't the dashboard. It was the capability to make better decisions with data.

Constraints

Team

1 Product Manager, no dedicated engineering capacity.

Resources

Existing databases, internal documentation, and AI-assisted prototyping.

Constraint

Prove the value of the system before asking for additional investment.

The constraint forced me to find the smallest intervention that could test the underlying idea before scaling the solution.

A closer look

A few reference screens from the system, not a polished showcase, just context for what this looked like in practice:

Outputs

  • Updated semantic foundation: a refreshed basic semantic layer, made available through the Data Lake so teams could work from shared product definitions and relationships.
  • Self-service data processes + skills: processes and reusable skills that reduced the dependency on a long centralized flow to define, instrument, and make product data available.
  • Data + context agent: a co-working agent designed not only to retrieve data, but to bring the context needed to understand what the signal means, why it matters, and how it can inform a product question.

Outcome

The biggest shift was moving from "making data available" to enabling better product decisions.

Instead of optimizing for the perfect dashboard, the system evolved toward giving teams the semantic context, interpretation guidance, and access they needed to understand evidence and act on it with greater autonomy.

How I used AI

AI acted as a co-pilot throughout the project, helping me structure the problem, interpret evidence, challenge assumptions, and prototype beyond my immediate role.

Product Ecosystem Cases

Reconciled at the Source

Solvo · Product Expansion Opportunity

Product Challenge

My challenge was to identify where Solvo could expand its product ecosystem, define a meaningful adjacent financial capability, and translate that opportunity into a scalable product proposal aligned with its ambition to become an all-in-one financial platform.

Full documentation on GitHub

What

A plug-and-play reconciliation engine turns that advantage into a scalable product: reusable templates for common reconciliation patterns, composable building blocks for customer-specific complexity, and AI layered on top of a deterministic core to configure, explain, and propose resolutions for exceptions. The result is an expansion of Solvo's value proposition: from executing financial transactions to delivering them reconciliation-ready, embedding Solvo deeper into how finance teams operate and close.

Why now

Before designing anything, three things from the research made the opportunity concrete.

  • Solvo already has an installed base of 5,000+ customers across 26 countries whose transaction data it already owns. Attaching reconciliation to that existing relationship is a natural extension, not a new business built from scratch.
  • The reconciliation software market is worth $2.5–4B and growing 12–15% a year, faster than financial close software overall, and the base-case model shows ~USD 24M in incremental annual revenue by year 3.
  • Finance teams spend 35–50 hours a month reconciling by hand, and industry-wide, normalization and chasing exceptions eat 40–60% of that effort: a large, well-documented pocket of manual work with a clear path to automate.

Competitors are already expanding into this

Clara (LatAm) already bundles a CFDI-linked accounting module into its card platform. Ramp and Brex both shipped AI-powered accounting agents in 2026.

AI reconciliation is becoming its own category

No longer a feature bolted onto close software: since 2024–2026 it started selling on its own, and over 90% of the category leader's eligible base already has AI enabled.

Mid-market is fragmented, and underserved

It's the fastest-growing segment in the whole reconciliation market, and the category leader is retreating from it.

How to build Reconciled at the Source: Product Proposal

The detail below is based on the working documentation in the repo. Some of it is still being built out. Expand a section, or go straight to the source.

Build proposal+
What to buildDescription
Deterministic engine The setup sequence (source, normalization, standardization, matching rules & tolerance), plus simulate, confirm, execute, and the diagnose/manage logic for Operación. Every step split into deterministic, human-decides, and AI-proposes.
Pilot instantiation (Cash Out) Pre-loaded matching rules for the side Solvo already owns: its own card data. This is what makes it a template.
Client-side AI-assisted intake Whenever the client uploads their books: what information is needed, help with parsing, suggested fixes. The same in both delivery models, not exclusive to either.
Agent interaction model Review and confirm through an agent + interface first. CLI/MCP is a valid path technically, but deliberately not the entry point: the roles who need to trust this first need visual, inspectable results.
MVP validation (skill) Package the engine as structured context for Claude or GPT and test it against real client data, before any custom interface exists. It's the fastest way to prove the matching and explanation logic holds up.
Operación in production Dashboards (integrity, summary, detailed, exceptions), managing the reconciliation run, managing pending items.

Reconciliation models: what the user would see+
  • AutomateReduce manual work. Automate repeatable reconciliation and focus teams on true exceptions.
  • UnifyKeep finance connected. Run transactions, reconciliation, and exception management in one workflow.
  • DetectCatch what needs attention. Surface anomalies and low-confidence items before they become close problems.
  • UnderstandUnderstand the why. Use AI to explain exceptions, suggest next steps, and support human decisions.
  • TrustTrace everything back to the source. Move from financial health to the exact transaction, evidence, and decision behind it.

Validation indicators+
Success metricPilot targetWhat it proves
Reconciliation Coverage ≥70% of eligible Solvo transactions routed through reconciliation We're converting the flow Solvo already originates into a new capability.
Paying Customer Adoption ≥30% of the rollout cohort live and paying The feature has enough value to drive commercial adoption.
Auto-Reconciliation Rate ≥80% reconciled without manual intervention The engine actually reduces operational load.
Rollout strategy+

Reconciliation Motor ships to the full installed base only after it's proven itself on a controlled first cohort. This follows directly from the engine's own design: the matching core is deterministic, so its rules and conditions must be validated against real client data before they run without close supervision. The rollout is the same trust-graduation mechanism the engine uses internally, applied once at the population level before it applies per account.

Key insight: every phase below draws from Solvo's existing installed base, not new client acquisition. Proving the engine on accounts that already trust Solvo with their transaction data is the lower-risk path. Using it to win new clients only makes sense once that trust is earned, not before.
PhaseWho, and why them first
Phase 1Promoters and Innovators: high NPS, proven loyalty, best positioned to absorb a rule still being tuned, and most likely to co-build rather than just consume. Gets a discount while the engine is validated on their data.
Phase 2Cohort expands once Phase 1's match rate and exception rate hit target.
Phase 3, general availabilityFull installed base, once rules are validated across enough real variation.
